messages.content: Can you help me find public libraries in New York, NY that have a Reading Room and Fiction section, and then in Los Angeles, CA that offer Wi-Fi and have a Children Section, and finally in Chicago, IL that have a Cafe and a Reading Room?

function.name: public_library_find_nearby
function.description: Locate nearby public libraries based on specific criteria like English fiction availability and Wi-Fi. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

location.description: The city and state, e.g. Boston, MA

facilities.description: Facilities and sections in public library.

We need to call the function public_library_find_nearby for each location with facilities. The user wants libraries in New York, NY with Reading Room and Fiction section. Then in Los Angeles, CA with Wi-Fi and Children Section. Then in Chicago, IL with Cafe and Reading Room.

We need to call the function three times. The function signature: public_library_find_nearby takes location string and facilities: one of the listed options. But facilities is a union type: "Wi-Fi" | "Reading Room" | "Fiction" | "Children Section" | "Cafe"[].

Wait: The type says facilities: "Wi-Fi" | "Reading Room" | "Fiction" | "Children Section" | "Cafe"[].

So facilities can be a string of one of those or an array of "Cafe"? That seems odd. Probably they want to pass an array of strings? But the type says "Cafe"[] meaning array of "Cafe". But maybe it's a mistake. We can pass an array of strings: ["Reading Room", "Fiction"] etc. But the type says union of string or array of "Cafe". That seems inconsistent. But we can try passing array of strings. The function might accept array of strings. Let's assume we can pass array of strings.

Thus we call:

public_library_find_nearby({"location":"New York, NY","facilities":["Reading Room","Fiction"]})

Similarly for LA: {"location":"Los Angeles, CA","facilities":["Wi-Fi","Children Section"]}

Chicago: {"location":"Chicago, IL","facilities":["Cafe","Reading Room"]}
